## Overview

The Tindi are an indigenous people of Dagestan in the North Caucasus. They live in five villages in the central area around the Andi-Koysu river and the surrounding mountains in northwestern southern Dagestan. Their language is Tindi, a Northeast Caucasian language, and they primarily follow Sunni Islam. The Tindi were counted as a distinct ethnic group in the Russian Census only in 1926, when 3,812 people reported being ethnic Tindis. In 1967, there were about 5,000 ethnic Tindi. Their language forms the basis of their ethnic identity, although its use is limited to domestic settings and is decreasing. The Tindi are culturally similar to the Avars and are in danger of assimilation by them.

## Language & religion

Tindi is a Northeast Caucasian language spoken in the Russian republic of Dagestan. Tindis have no individual designation for their language; people living in the village of Idar call it *Idarab mitstsi*, meaning “the language of the Idar village.” Tindi is only an oral language, while Avar or Russian are used in written communication. It has approximately 4,500 speakers, and its vocabulary contains loanwords from Avar, Turkish, Arabic, and Russian. Tindi is typically unwritten; a 2003 dictionary uses an orthography. The language has 20 phonemic vowels, and nasalized vowels may also exist. The Tindi primarily follow Sunni Islam.
